title: Pointer arithmetic
relevance: Checks that candidates know pointers move by element size, which is the basis for correctly walking arrays in C/C++.

phases.goal: Establish that pointer arithmetic counts elements of the pointed-to type, not raw bytes.

must_hit.point: Pointer arithmetic is defined in terms of the elements a pointer points at, not in raw bytes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says adding to a pointer advances by elements of its type, whatever that element's size is.

must_hit.point: Adding one to a pointer advances it to the next element of its type.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States that +1 means next element, not +1 byte.

must_hit.point: An array name decays to the address of its first element, so a pointer can act as a cursor through the array.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions int* p = A pointing at A[0] because the array name decays to that address.

probes: What does it mean that pointer arithmetic is defined in terms of elements rather than bytes?
If p points at A[0], what does p + 1 refer to?

hints.1: Think about what ‘next’ means for a typed pointer, not a raw address.
hints.2: Relate the step size to the pointed-to type’s element width.
hints.3: p++ / +1 moves to the next element of that type; the array name decays to &A[0].

phases.goal: Show how increments, integer adds, and pointer subtraction are scaled by element size.

must_hit.point: The compiler scales every pointer addition by the size of the pointed-to type: p++ does not add 1 to the address; it adds 1 × sizeof(*p).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly contrasts ‘add 1 to the address’ with adding 1 × sizeof(*p).

must_hit.point: Integer offsets jump by element counts: e.g. from address 200, p+2 lands on 206 for 2-byte ints (four bytes), or advances eight bytes for 4-byte ints—always two elements.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the table/example: p++, p--, p+2, p-2 move among 200/202/206 in element steps.

must_hit.point: Subtracting two pointers into the same array yields how many elements apart they are (not bytes); the sign records direction.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives q-p = 3 and p-q = -3, and notes division by element size is automatic.

probes: If each int is 2 bytes and p holds 200, what address does p+2 produce, and why?
What does q - p mean when p and q point into the same array?

hints.1: Ask whether the machine adds the integer you wrote, or a scaled offset.
hints.2: Separate addition/increment (move by N elements) from subtraction of two pointers (count elements between).
hints.3: p++ adds 1×sizeof(*p); q-p is (address gap)/sizeof(int), so 206-200 with 2-byte ints gives 3, and the sign shows ahead vs behind.

tradeoffs.topic: Element-scaled pointer steps vs raw byte offsets
tradeoffs.strong_answer: All pointer arithmetic—increment, adding an integer, and subtracting two pointers—counts in elements; addresses move in multiples of the pointed-to type’s size so a pointer can step cleanly from one array element to the next, rather than by raw bytes.

gotchas.trap: Assuming p++ adds 1 to the stored address.
gotchas.correction: p++ adds 1 × sizeof(*p), advancing one element of the pointed-to type.

gotchas.trap: Assuming pointer subtraction returns a byte distance.
gotchas.correction: The language reports the gap in elements; e.g. addresses 206 and 200 with 2-byte ints yield 3, and the sign shows which pointer is ahead.
